title: the sounds
hook: Krishna written in Devanagari, and the i that isn't there
tomorrow: if one wrong sound can spoil a mantra, what about a sincere heart?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sounds off Shiva's drum: lists so tidy that one short word, ac, names every vowel. The second line of that list holds today's puzzle.

Krishna. In English letters the name has an i, right after the r. Write it in Devanagari, कृष्ण, and the i is gone. There's a k with a small hook hanging under it, then the rest of the name. No i anywhere. The same thing happens in rishi, a seer. In the Rig Veda, the collection of hymns. In amrita, the drink of immortality. Each one is spelled in English with ri, and in Devanagari with no i at all. Nothing is misspelled. So where did it go?
screen: `KRISHNA HAS AN I.` → `कृष्ण DOESN'T.` → `RISHI, RIG VEDA, AMRITA.`

segments.voice: Here's the answer. That little hook under the k isn't an r plus a vowel. It is the vowel. Sanskrit has an r that can carry a syllable on its own, the way a or i does. In Roman letters, scholars write it as an r with a small dot underneath. And it's right there on Shiva's drum: the second line of the list is this r, and an l that works the same way, filed among the vowels before e and o. So Krishna is really two beats: kr, then shna. Rishi is r, then shi. How is it said? English has something close: the r in a cold brrr, held with no vowel around it. Over time, speakers have leaned on a little vowel to make it easier. Some say ri: KRISH-nuh. Others say something closer to ru: KRUSH-nuh. Same letter, same name, traveling through different mouths. And here's the detail worth telling a friend: a Sanskrit dictionary files this r with the vowels, right after u, not under r. So when an English spelling shows ri in a Sanskrit word, check the Devanagari before you go looking. It may be one vowel in disguise.
screen: `THE HOOK IS THE VOWEL.` · `AN R THAT CARRIES A SYLLABLE.` · `RI IN SOME MOUTHS, RU IN OTHERS.` · `FILED WITH THE VOWELS, AFTER U.` · then, large: `ONE VOWEL IN DISGUISE.`

segments.voice: Say brrr softly, and hold the r with no vowel around it, the way you might on a cold morning. Then let that same r carry a word, slowly: rrr-shi, krrr-shna, feeling the tongue hold the beat on its own. When it feels steady, let the mouth go quiet and breathe.
The sounds: today, the r that is a vowel, hiding in Krishna, rishi and the Rig Veda.
Your line: the sounds. Some of them hide inside English spellings, and the Devanagari gives them away. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sanskrit teachers introduce this vowel, written ऋ, alongside a, i and u, and Hindus pronounce it in more than one way depending on where they learned it, closer to ri or closer to ru.

original.note: Sanskrit: ṛṣi, a seer. It opens with the vowel ṛ, written ऋ, with no separate i.
